titulo.texto: Mural “Procession in the Mixteca,” by Arturo Estrada

frase_gancho.texto: A student of Frida Kahlo painted a procession of faith in Oaxaca.

puente_narrativo.texto: From the procession, we move on to the dance. Look for an enormous headdress of colorful feathers, shaped like a fan or a half circle and trimmed with ribbons, made to be danced in and not only to be looked at.

guion_corto.texto: This mural was painted in 1964 by Arturo Estrada, an artist born in 1925 in Panindícuaro, Michoacán. He was a student of Diego Rivera and Frida Kahlo, and one of the four “Fridos.” Titled “Procession in the Mixtec Region,” and also known as “Pedimento o manda,” it portrays a devotional pilgrimage linked to the shrine of the Virgin of Juquila. A pedimento is a request for a favor, and a manda is the promise made in return. It was painted for this ethnography hall, when the museum was getting ready to open in September 1964.

guion_largo.texto:
“Pedimento” and “manda” are two words from popular faith. A pedimento is asking a saint or a virgin for a favor. A manda is the promise made in return, such as going on a pilgrimage to their shrine. It is the same idea you saw in the highlands of Puebla, where many people dance the Danza de los Quetzales because of a manda. And it is one of the names of this mural.

Because this mural has several names. Its inaugural title from 1964 is “Procession in the Mixtec Region.” The painter himself, in his memoirs, remembers it as “Religious Life among the Mixtec.” And an INAH record lists it, also in 1964, as “Pedimento o manda.” It seems to be the same work, and all three names speak of faith.

It was painted by Arturo Estrada, who was born in 1925 in Panindícuaro, a town in Michoacán. At the age of fifteen he went to Mexico City and entered La Esmeralda, the art school where Diego Rivera and Frida Kahlo taught. He was one of the four “Fridos.” He helped Rivera with the mosaics of the Anahuacalli and taught at La Esmeralda for more than forty years. In 2025 he turned one hundred.

Frida taught with questions, not with theories. One of them was how many colors you can see in a tree. Estrada later recalled that she took them to Teotihuacán, because she said artists should study their roots. That lesson traveled far: years later, Estrada painted for a museum devoted precisely to those roots.

His fellow artist Arturo García Bustos, the painter of the mural you just saw, was another of the “Fridos.” Both painted for this hall. With the same teacher, they created two ways of telling the story of Oaxaca: one through its people and regions, the other through its faith.

The scene portrays a moment from the festivities of the Virgin of Juquila. Her shrine is in Santa Catarina Juquila, in southwestern Oaxaca. Every December 8, thousands of pilgrims arrive, many of them from municipalities within the state itself, to ask for a favor. The catalog title speaks of the Mixtec Region. But devotion to Juquila brings together people from all over Oaxaca.

Estrada learned the craft in the mural painting course that Rivera gave in 1943. A mural, unlike a painting on canvas, is conceived for a wall and for many people at once. For this subject it needs no heroes or battles. A crowd walking in the same direction is enough. That is why it is best to look at the whole before each face: a procession reads as a single body moving forward, at a slow pace and with a shared purpose. A pilgrimage costs days of walking and weariness, and that is why a manda is not just a phrase: it is an act carried out with the body.

Before moving on, look for the people walking together. Where are they headed? Are they carrying flowers, candles, or an image? A procession is, in the end, a way of asking together.

texto: Look for the people walking together: where are they headed?
Notice whether anyone is carrying flowers, candles, or a sacred image
Look at the clothing and the landscape: what tells you that you are in Oaxaca?

texto.Author: Arturo Estrada (born in 1925)
texto.Work: “Procession in the Mixtec Region” (also recorded as “Pedimento o manda”)
texto.Theme: Pilgrimage and communal religiosity in Oaxaca

texto.pregunta: Myth: Pilgrimages and mandas are customs of the past.
texto.respuesta: Reality: Every December, thousands of people arrive at the shrine of the Virgin of Juquila, in Oaxaca, to ask for a favor; the tradition evoked by the mural is still alive.
